newsitem.title: UK: Strong stg - the worst is yet to come for exporters.
newsitem.headline: Strong stg - the worst is yet to come for exporters.

text.p: British exporters will feel yet more pain when the full impact of pound strength filters through into corporate results this summer, but should breathe a sigh of relief later this year when sterling is expected to ease to more comfortable levels, analysts said on Friday.

Anglo-Dutch publisher Reed Elsevier and international news and information provider Reuters this week joined the chorus of companies and industry organisations bemoaning the effects of the strong pound.
Experts warn, however, that things are likely to get worse before they get better, because export contracts are often signed six to 12 months in advance.

"The full impact of the pound's strength is likely to be felt later in the year, but the prospect of a weakening sterling and an improvement in the economy of continental European export markets should provide some relief," said Stephen Davies, economic research executive at the Institute of Directors (IOD).
Since last August, sterling has risen from around 2.30 marks to 2.80 now, its highest level since Britain left the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.

"Exporters are going to get some relief from an expected weakening of the pound towards the end of the year but the worst is yet to come in the coming months," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

The powerful pound has dealt a double blow to many companies. A large proportion - almost 40 percent - of British corporate profits come from overseas, and sterling strength makes products more expensive abroad. It also has a monetary tightening effect.
The pound's trade-weighted index, incorporating the currencies of major trading partners, rose 15 percent in 1996 and is up about four percent since the start of this year.
Sterling's rise is likely to accelerate cost-efficiency measures, and might even be responsible for future job cuts, analysts said.

"If sterling remains at its current level, there has to be a concern that export performance is further threatened and import penetration of the home market will rise, unless British industry can cut its cost base further," said Graham Mackenzie, director-general of the Engineering Employers Federation.

British Steel has been hit by a series of profit downgrades by major investment houses this month. The company generates about 55 percent of its profits abroad, and is particularly vulnerable to rises in sterling/mark because of the size of the German steel market, the biggest in Europe.

"The strength of sterling is having an adverse effect on our prices and profits," a British Steel spokesman said. "Because Germany is the largest steel-producing nation and the largest consumer of steel in Europe, we have to take into account at what level steel is priced there," he added.

But forecasters see the the pound's meteoric rise coming to an end. Even though the prospect of strong economic growth and higher interest rates is keeping sterling firm now, it is likely to weaken if rates go up less than expected.
An increasing perception that the worst may be over for the German economy, Britain's dominant trading partner in the European Union, will also weigh on the pound.
"The foreign exchange market hasn't yet fully taken on board evidence that continental Europe seems to be recovering, which reduces the chances of interest rate cuts there," said Davies at the IOD.
The pound's favourable yield differentials with other European markets have been the backbone of the rally.
"Towards the end of the year sterling is likely to weaken because of Britain's worsening trading position and if interest rates don't rise as much as expected," said HSBC's David.

A Reuters poll of more than 20 currency forecasters published last week showed that on average the pound is expected to drift back to around 2.60 marks at the end of the year, with levels around 2.50 seen in late 1998.
